contested.text: The four opened records on the Olson death disagree: a tenth floor or tenth story window, or thirteen stories; 27 or 28 November 1953. The Rockefeller Commission says two CIA employees were reprimanded, while the 2012 complaint says no formal reprimands were issued.

The official account carried its own qualification: the Rockefeller report footnoted that the few remaining Agency records indicated Olson may have had a history of emotional instability. The murder allegation is the 2012 complaint's, and it was dismissed on timeliness, waiver and sovereign immunity, not on its truth.

The records disagree on the scale of MKULTRA: Turner gave 80 institutions from the recovered files, while the hearing's own opening statement says eighty-six universities or institutions were involved.

The opened records contradict the podcast versions. BLUEBIRD's founding document is dated 1950, is signed inside the CIA, concerns defectors and agents rather than children, and the programme was renamed before MKULTRA existed; no record shows Gottlieb running MKULTRA from 1953; the search for the MKULTRA files was done inside the Agency in response to Marks's request; the AZORIAN history names Lockheed as one of four consortium members with no lease or term, and never mentions any underwater reconnaissance office; Cabell was still in the Air Force when Blue Book began, and resigned rather than being dismissed.
No opened record bears on O'Neill's account of Gottlieb and Louis Jolyon West, and the released Subproject 43 file names no researcher.

The records do not show Smith approving a psychological use of the subject: the approval lines on the Psychological Strategy Board recommendation are blank, and his own draft proposed scientific research.

Hillenkoetter's claims had contemporary critics and no support in his FBI files. The 1960 Enquirer editorial said it could not agree with him that the Air Force was deceiving the public, and a text search of his FBI files found no mention of NICAP, flying saucers or the year 1960, though the scans are uneven.

The contractor custody claims are denied: AARO states that executives and chief technology officers of the named companies denied the allegations to its Director on the record. Linking the 1978 Lockheed of the AZORIAN history to today's Lockheed Martin is an identification across the 1995 merger that the document does not make.

lead.text: The CIA's own records show it running programmes outside its normal controls and then losing or destroying the paper: MKULTRA was authorised with normal approval, funding and accounting procedures waived, its files were destroyed on a verbal order in January 1973, and what survived was found only because a FOIA request sent Agency staff into the retired records. This topic carries that case, the death of Frank Olson and Project AZORIAN as documented precedents for concealment.

record.text: BLUEBIRD's founding memorandum set up interrogation teams of a psychiatrist, a polygraph-hypnotist and a technician to use the polygraph, drugs and hypnotism, with a Washington doctor's office as cover for training and experimentation, on a one-year budget of $65,515. It was addressed to the Director of Central Intelligence, whom the National Security Archive's catalogue identifies as Hillenkoetter.

By July 1952 the Security Office was reporting ARTICHOKE's operational use to the Director: suspected Russian double agents interrogated under a psychiatric-medical cover by narcosis and hypnosis, one session followed by a total amnesia produced by post-hypnotic suggestion.

The Inspector General's 1963 survey states MKULTRA's purpose as research and development of chemical, biological and radiological materials to control human behaviour in clandestine operations, records that Dulles authorised it in 1953, and says normal procedures for project approval, funding and accounting were waived.

Gottlieb's signature is on the money: as Chief of the Technical Services Staff Chemical Division he certified the invoices of MKULTRA Subproject 43 in March and June 1955. The 1963 Inspector General calls him Deputy Chief of the Technical Services Division, and the 1973 destruction order came from him as its Chief.

What survived did so by accident. DCI Stansfield Turner told the Senate in 1977 of seven boxes found at the Retired Records Center, sent there by the Budget and Fiscal Section in 1970 in a departure from normal procedure whose reason was not known, which is how they escaped the 1973 destruction and the 1975 searches. A 1977 CIA memorandum adds that Gottlieb had destroyed every MKULTRA document he could locate.

The CIA's own memorandum of 22 June 1977 says the search that found the boxes was made because of John Marks's FOIA request F-76-374, then in litigation, and that the recovered material included the original memorandum setting up MKULTRA over Dulles's signature. It recommended telling the Senate Select Committee before telling Marks's attorneys; the Senate later said one individual, through a FOIA request, accomplished what two Senate committees could not.

The recovered finance files cover 149 numbered subprojects. Turner told the committee they named 185 non-government researchers and assistants and 80 institutions, including 44 colleges or universities, 12 hospitals or clinics and 3 penal institutions.

The Rockefeller Commission disclosed the Olson death in June 1975 without naming him. It records that the General Counsel ruled the death arose out of an experiment in the course of his official duties, securing death benefits, and that the Director reprimanded two CIA employees. The Church Committee text names Robert Lashbrook and Sidney Gottlieb as running the experiment, and says neither the Chief of the Technical Services Staff nor the Deputy Director for Plans specifically authorised it.

Private Law 94-126 paid Alice Olson and her three children $187,500 each in full settlement, on condition that all of them waived any rights arising from the death. President Ford signed it on 12 October 1976 and said his administration had supported $1,250,000.

The children's 2012 suit, brought in the District of Columbia, was dismissed in 2013 as untimely, waived by the prior settlement and outside the government's waiver of sovereign immunity. The opinion noted that the public record supports many of the allegations, farfetched as they may sound.

AZORIAN's released history records CIA sponsorship for intelligence collection, the participation of Hughes Tool Company, the Summa Corporation and Global Marine, and facts acknowledged in tax, FOIA and patent litigation. It closes with a private consortium including Lockheed, Global Marine, Standard Oil of Indiana and Royal Dutch Shell readying the ship for deep-ocean mining from late 1978.

On the flying saucer subject, Smith directed on 20 August 1952 that a National Security Council intelligence directive be prepared, and a draft memorandum over his name proposed a coordinated scientific research effort. The recommendation that he take the subject to the Psychological Strategy Board carries blank approval lines on the released copy.

The Robertson Panel was convened by the CIA's Office of Scientific Intelligence and met from 14 to 18 January 1953. It recommended a public education programme with training and debunking aims through mass media, canvassed the Disney organisation and the Navy Special Devices Center, and recommended monitoring civilian UFO groups. The Agency's historian records that any mention of CIA sponsorship of the panel was forbidden.

Dulles's three signed letters of 13 March 1953 sent the panel report to the Secretary of Defense and two civil agencies, said its conclusions pointed to certain potential dangers to national security, said the Agency did not consider the subject primarily its concern, and attributed the panel to General Smith. Each letter is a rewrite of an earlier version that was not sent.

The Agency's in-house historian, Gerald K. Haines, published an account of the CIA's role in the study of UFOs from 1947 to 1990 in 1997, and the CIA describes its public UFO collection as mostly foreign-press cables and internal memos on handling public inquiries.

The instruments behind all of this are signed. Truman's directive of 22 January 1946 created the post of Director of Central Intelligence, barred police or internal security functions and made the Director responsible for protecting sources and methods; the National Security Act of 1947 created the Agency under the National Security Council and let it perform such other functions as the Council may direct.

Charles P. Cabell was the Air Force's Director of Intelligence to 1953 and then Deputy Director of Central Intelligence; the CIA's chronology records his resignation on 27 December 1961, effective 31 January 1962.

The Agency and the Atomic Energy Commission corresponded at the top: Dulles thanked AEC Chairman Glenn Seaborg in October 1961 for a report he was circulating inside the Agency, and in 1963 Seaborg sent the Commission's annual report to Director John McCone.

summary.text: The behavioural programmes began by going round the Agency's own review. Project BLUEBIRD was submitted directly to the Director of Central Intelligence on 5 April 1950 rather than through the Projects Review Committee, with knowledge restricted to the absolute minimum number of persons; it was renamed ARTICHOKE in August 1951, and MKULTRA was authorised by Allen Dulles in April 1953.

MKULTRA kept no records of the planning and approval of its test programmes, according to its own Inspector General, and in January 1973 its files were destroyed on the verbal orders of Sidney Gottlieb, who testified that he was carrying out the verbal order of Director Helms.

The death of Frank Olson, dosed with LSD without his knowledge at a 1953 meeting of Army and CIA scientists, is what made the cryptonym public in 1975. Congress compensated his family by private law in 1976, and the family's 2012 suit was dismissed in 2013 without reaching the merits.

Project AZORIAN shows a different technique: covert recovery of foreign hardware under commercial cover. The Agency's own history says a Soviet submarine lost in March 1968 was brought up on 8 August 1974 in a system built for the mission, and that the facts later acknowledged in court still leave the purpose, success, other participants, technology and funding under continuing prohibition.

The same Agency handled the flying saucer subject in the same years. Director Walter Bedell Smith directed an intelligence effort in August 1952, the Robertson Panel was convened in January 1953 with any mention of CIA sponsorship forbidden, and Dulles then told three agencies the subject was not primarily the CIA's concern.

title: CIA secrecy precedents: MKULTRA, the Olson death and Azorian
